content:
Induction looks like a proof topic. But JEE turns it into fast objective marks. The trick is the step from P(k) to P(k+1). Add the wrong term there, and the answer breaks. So take the free JEE Mathematical Induction online test below. It has 15 exam-style MCQs. Scoring is instant. Every answer shows the term you add. Aim for 12 out of 15.

What JEE asks from Mathematical Induction

  • The term you add from P(k) to P(k+1).
  • Closed-form sums like cubes and odd numbers.
  • Divisibility results for every natural number.
  • Recurrence relations solved by a guessed rule.
  • Steps that skip, so only odd or even n hold.

Formulas and facts to revise first

  • The cubes sum to (n(n+1)/2) squared.
  • The first n odd numbers add to n squared.
  • The squares sum to n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.
  • Prove the base case before the step.
  • For divisibility, test small n to spot the divisor.

Mistakes that cost JEE marks

  • Students add the kth term, not the (k+1)th term.
  • Many skip the base case, so the chain never starts.
  • A P(k) to P(k+2) jump covers only one parity.

Free Mathematical Induction online test for JEE

The 15 questions below come from our verified JEE bank. Attempt each one. Then press Check my score. Read the working for anything you miss. This JEE Mathematical Induction online test drills the step JEE Main loves.

How to score full marks here

Read the sum or the claim first. Spot the (k+1)th term you must add. Then add it to P(k) and simplify. Match the result to the target form. For a divisibility item, test small n first. That single habit clears most induction MCQs. So practise the step until it feels automatic.

Practise the whole chapter

Want more than a quiz? The JEE Maths DPP Mathematical Induction e-book drills the full chapter. It costs Rs 49. Every sheet ends with an answer key. Every question shows a clean step. You can also browse the JEE Maths DPP shelf. For theory first, try the JEE Maths course at vidaara.org. It covers induction free.

questions.q: You prove by induction that 1³ + 2³ + ... + n³ = (n(n+1)/2)². The value of the sum for n = 14 is:
questions.explanation: Put n = 14 in the closed form: (14·15/2)² = 105² = 11025.

questions.q: P(1) is true and P(k) implies P(k+2) for every natural k. Then P(n) is certainly true for:
questions.explanation: Starting from P(1), the step reaches P(3), P(5) and so on. So only the odd numbers are guaranteed.

questions.q: While proving 1³ + 2³ + ... + n³ = (n(n+1)/2)² by induction, the term added going from P(11) to P(12) is:
questions.explanation: The extra term is (k+1)³ at k = 11, so it is 12³ = 1728.

In proving 1² + 2² + ... + n² = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 by induction, which term must you add to pass from P(k) to P(k+1)?
questions.explanation: The (k+1)th term of the series is (k+1)². Add it to P(k) to complete the step.

questions.q: By induction, for every natural number n, the expression 6^(2n) - 35n - 1 is divisible by:
questions.explanation: Test n = 1: 36 - 35 - 1 = 0, and n = 2: 1296 - 70 - 1 = 1225. So 1225 divides it for all n.

questions.q: In proving 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n-1) = n² by induction, which term must you add to pass from P(k) to P(k+1)?
questions.explanation: The (k+1)th odd number is 2k+1. Add it to P(k), and k² + (2k+1) = (k+1)².

questions.explanation: The extra term is (k+1)³ at k = 9, so it is 10³ = 1000.

faq.q: Is induction asked in JEE Main or Advanced?
faq.a: Induction shows up in JEE Main, usually as an objective question on the induction step or a divisibility result. This test matches that pattern.

faq.q: What is the single most common induction error?
faq.a: Adding the kth term instead of the (k+1)th term during the step. Get the added term right and most of the chapter falls into place.
